dva-avc-205.text: A team realizes that a small percentage of requests to a API based on Lambda has significantly higher latency (e. g..: 1200ms) compared to the typical ~80ms. They suspect that these slow requests correspond to COLD STARTS (start-up of a new running environment). They have X-Ray Active Tracing enabled. CONFIRMAR, for a specific slow track, if the additional latency is attributable to a cold start, instead of, for example, a slow downstream?
options: Compare the 'Duration' metric of the slow invocation with the 'Duration' metric of the fast invocations — if the difference is exactly the same as the timeout timeout of the function, the cold start is confirmed.
Check metric CloudWatch 'CompetitiveExecutions' at the time of slow requisition — a value of CompetitiveExecutions equal to 1 confirms that it was a cold start.

In the timeline/details of the X-Ray track for slow requisition, look for an 'Initiation' subsegment (sometimes shown as a distinct segment/phase before the main segment 'Invocation') — X-Ray automatically records the duration of the FASE OF INIT of the Lambda (runtime loading, execution of code outside the handler, e.g.: module level imports/connections) as a separate subsegment when a cold start occurs; if this subsegment Initiation is present and corresponds to a significant part of the 1200ms.: 1000ms), latency is attributable to the initialization of the cold start; if absent, the invocation was 'warm' and extra latency comes from another place (e.g. a subsegment called downstream).
Enable Lambda Insights and check the metric 'memory_utilization' — a value of memory usage close to 100% at the time of the request confirms that the additional latency was caused by cold initiation.
dva-avc-205.explanation: Right. Lambda Active Tracking is enabled and a cold start occurs, X-Ray automatically records FASE INITIATING (Init) — loading of the runtime and execution of the initialization code outside the handler — as a distinct 'Initiation' subsegment in the timeline of the trace, with its own duration. The presence and duration of this subsegment confirm directly whether and how much, the cold start contributed to the total latency of the slow request; its absence indicates a warm invocation, pointing to another cause (e.g., called downstream)).
dva-avc-205.hint: Think about what stage of implementation of the Lambda the X-Ray records as a distinct subsegment, separated from the main subsegment of invocation, specifically when a cold start occurs..
optionRationales: Right. Lambda Active Tracking is enabled and a cold start occurs, X-Ray automatically records FASE INITIATING (Init) — loading of the runtime and execution of the initialization code outside the handler — as a distinct 'Initiation' subsegment in the timeline of the trace, with its own duration. The presence and duration of this subsegment confirm directly whether and how much, the cold start contributed to the total latency of the slow request; its absence indicates a warm invocation, pointing to another cause (e.g., called downstream)).

Incorrect. 'ConcurrentExecutions' reflects the NUMBER of simultaneous invocations at one point in time, not if a SPECIFIC invocation was a cold start; a value equal to 1 does not confirm cold start (a warm and reused environment could also be the only one running at that time), and a higher value does not rule out a cold start occurring competing with others.

Incorrect. The 'Duration' metric of Lambda DO NOT report separately the time of initialization of cold start in a way that can be isolated by comparing it with the value of TIMEOUT (an unrelated configuration parameter); the X-Ray initialization subsegment is the mechanism that specifically isolates the duration of the init phase..

Incorrect. High memory usage indicates MEMORY PRESSURE (possibly causing garbage collection or throttling breaks), which is a problem DIFERENTE of the initialization time of cold start; does not confirm or measure the duration of FASE OF INIT that the subsegment 'Initiation' of X-Ray isolates.

dva-avc-206.text: Functions Lambda of a team currently record log messages in unstructured text (e.g.: 'Processing order 12345 for customer ABC, total $99.99'). The team wants to make these fields TRUSTABLE and EFICIENTEMENTE searchable at Logs Insights DAQUI PARA FRENTE, without depending on parsing the writing of the free text. Continue with free text logging, but standardize all messages to follow EXATAMENTE the same string template (including spacing), and then use SEMPRE the same 'parse' pattern fixed in all Logs Insights queries.

Adopt LOGGING ESTRUTURADO: perform the functions Lambda issuing log entries as objects JSON with NOMES OF CAMPO explicit and consistent (e.g. {"level"": "INFO", "message: "Processing order", "orderId": "12345", "user": "ABC", "total": 99.99}) instead of strings in free text. CloudWatch Logs Insights DESCOBRE AUTOMATICAMENTE log event fields in format JSON, making queries like 'stats sum(total) by customerId' possible SEM no expression 'parse', and immune to changes in the writing of any field 'message''.
dva-avc-206.explanation: Right. Lambda emit logs as objects JSON with fields explicitly named, or CloudWatch Logs Insights automatically detects and exposes these fields for queries (referenced by name, e.g. orderId, customerId, total), allowing direct aggregations such as 'stats sum(total) by customerId' without any expression 'parse'. POR NOME (not by position/free text writing), small changes in the string of a message do not break the queries — solving directly the fragility described.
dva-avc-206.hint: Think about which log format allows Logs Insights to automatically discover and view fields by name instead of extracting them from positions within a free text string.
optionRationales: Right. Lambda emit logs as objects JSON with fields explicitly named, or CloudWatch Logs Insights automatically detects and exposes these fields for queries (referenced by name, e.g. orderId, customerId, total), allowing direct aggregations such as 'stats sum(total) by customerId' without any expression 'parse'. POR NOME (not by position/free text writing), small changes in the string of a message do not break the queries — solving directly the fragility described.

Incorrect. This approach is fragile by design: it requires perfect and continuous discipline from all developers to maintain an exact string template (any deviation breaks the 'parse' pattern) — exactly the maintenance burden that the team wants to eliminate. JSON eliminates this fragility using explicitly named fields instead of parsing text positional.

Incorrect. EMF is specifically for issuing METRICS CUSTOMIZADAS (numeric values to be displayed/alarmed in CloudWatch Metrics) from log data, via a specific metadata structure '_aws' — is not a general mechanism to make arbitrary free text fields searchable in Logs Insights; this is what structured logging in JSON (independent of EMF) provides.

Incorrect. CloudWatch Logs Anomaly Detection identifies the Fathers INCOMUNS in the volume/content of logs for alert purposes, but does not extract/retroactive or automatically indexes CAMPOS Arbitrariness (orderId, customerId) of free text messages for general consultation — structured logging with explicit field names is the direct solution.

dva-avc-207.text: A function AWS Lambda processes an event source of DynamoDB The team realizes that the metric CloudWatch 'IteratorAge' of this function is AUMENTANDO CONSTANTEMENTE (in several hours), indicating that the function is delayed in the processing of the stream — new stream records take hours to be processed after they occur. Which configuration in the event source mapping solves this, allowing the stream to advance beyond the problem log while still trying to process it separately?
options: Configure 'BisectBatchOnFunctionError' = true in event source mapping of DynamoDB Streams (combined with a reasonable 'MaximumRetryAttempts' and/or 'MaximumRecordAgeInSeconds', and optionally a 'OnFailure' Destination for a DLQ) — when the function fails to process a batch, BisectBatchOnFunctionError does the Lambda DIVIDIR the batch that failed in two smaller batches and try each separately, bisecting recursively until the batches succeed or are reduced to ONE REGISTRO — isolating the problem record (which can then be sent to a DLQ via the Fault Destination after MaximumRetryAttempts, allowing the iterator to advance beyond it) without blocking the entire shard indefinitely because of a single bad record mixed with good records.

dva-avc-207.explanation: Right. BisectBatchOnFunctionError does the Lambda recursively divide a batch that failed in smaller batches until isolating the problematic log(s) in a batch of size 1; combined with MaximumRetryAttempts and a Destination OnFailure for DLQ, the isolated problem record can be sent to DLQ after exhausting the attempts, allowing IteratorAge to decrease again as the shard advances beyond it — without indefinitely blocking the subsequent records that would be processed normally.
dva-avc-207.hint: Think about which configuration does the Lambda DIVIDIR a batch that failed in smaller parts and try each part separately instead of holding the whole batch indefinitely.
optionRationales: Right. BisectBatchOnFunctionError does the Lambda recursively divide a batch that failed in smaller batches until isolating the problematic log(s) in a batch of size 1; combined with MaximumRetryAttempts and a Destination OnFailure for DLQ, the isolated problem record can be sent to DLQ after exhausting the attempts, allowing IteratorAge to decrease again as the shard advances beyond it — without indefinitely blocking the subsequent records that would be processed normally.

Incorrect. A BatchSize MAIOR Makes the Problem PIOR, no better: a bigger batch containing the problematic record would make a set AINDA MAIOR of records to be retained/locked together; this is the opposite of the necessary bisection approach.

Incorrect. ParallelFactor allows MULTIPLES BATCHES CONCORRENTES of the MESMO shard are processed in parallel (useful for THROUGHPUT when processing is independent and the order inside the shard is not strictly necessary), but does not help a specific batch that is PRESO in retreats due to a bad record inside it — this specific batch continues to block its own sequence; the bisection is what isolates the problematic record.

Incorrect. Event source mappings of DynamoDB Streams (based on polling/pull) do not use the concept of 'Visibility Timeout' in style SQS for this purpose; retreats/bisection/routing for DLQ on stream-based origins are governed by MaximumRetryAttempts, BisectBatchOnFunctionError, MaximumRecordAgeInSeconds and Destinations OnFailure — not by a visibility timeout configuration.

dva-avc-208.text: One API WebSocket of API Gateway uses integrations Lambda for the $connect, $disconnect and a custom route 'sendMessage', with the connections stored in a table DynamoDB (mapping connectionId for user/session information by the $connect handler, and removed by $disconnect. The correct treatment is to capture this exception at the time of PostToConnection and use it as a SINAL to exclude the obsolete entry from the table DynamoDB, keeping the table consistent (self-corrective cleaning) instead of trying to forward to a connection that no longer exists.

The correct treatment is to capture this exception at the time of PostToConnection and use it as a SINAL to exclude the obsolete entry from the table DynamoDB, keeping the table consistent (self-corrective cleaning) instead of trying to forward to a connection that no longer exists.

dva-avc-211.text: An on-call engineer is setting up alarms from CloudWatch for a function AWS Lambda critical and wants alarms that distinguish between THREE different fault modes: (1) the function code itself is launching exceptions/returning errors; (2) the function is being REJEITADA to execute due to competition limits; and (3) the function is performing successfully, but taking longer than expected (possible performance degradation). CloudWatch correspond to these three different fault modes, and how the alarms should be configured to distinguish them.?
options: Configure a single composite alarm combining 'Errors', 'Throttles' and 'Duration' with OR logic, since either of the three conditions indicates that something is wrong and needs the same remedial response.
Use the 'ConcurrentExecutions' metric to detect code errors, 'IteratorAge' to detect throttling, and 'Errors' to detect performance degradation.

Use only the 'Invocations' metric with three alarms at different thresholds (low, medium, high), since different Invocations thresholds correspond to code errors, throttling and performance degradation, respectively.

(1) Metric 'ERRORS' — counts invocations in which the function code returned an error (untreated exception, or, for asynchronous invocations, error responses); an alarm in Errors (e.g.: Errors > 0, or error rate = Errors/Invocations > threshold) indicates FALHAS AT CODE LEVEL. (2) Metric 'THROTTLES' — claim account REJEITADAS for exceeding competition limits (TooManyRequestsException)) ANTES even the function code execute; an alarm in Throttles > 0 indicates a competition problem/CAPACIDADE, other than code errors. (3) Metric 'DURATION' — o TEMPO EXECUTION OF successful invocations; an alarm in Duration (e.g. p99 from Duration approaching the configured timeout) indicates DEGRADATION OF PERFORMANCE, These three metrics are emitted independently and should have alarms SEPARADOS, since each one points to a different remedy.
dva-avc-211.explanation: Correct. Errors measure flaws. DENTRO the execution of the code (exceptions/errors returned by the function); 'Throttles' measures invocations REJEITADAS ANTES of the code to execute, by limit of competition; 'Duration' measures the time of execution of successful invocations. Each metric points to a different root cause and remedy — correct code bugs, increase competition/reserved competition, or optimize performance/investigation slow dependencies, respectively — so they must have separate alarms instead of being combined.
dva-avc-211.hint: Think of three metrics of the Lambda which measure, respectively: failures within code execution, rejections ANTES of the execution code, and the time that successful execution takes.
optionRationales: Correct. Errors measure flaws. DENTRO the execution of the code (exceptions/errors returned by the function); 'Throttles' measures invocations REJEITADAS ANTES of the code to execute, by limit of competition; 'Duration' measures the time of execution of successful invocations. Each metric points to a different root cause and remedy — correct code bugs, increase competition/reserved competition, or optimize performance/investigation slow dependencies, respectively — so they must have separate alarms instead of being combined.

Incorrect. 'Invocations' simply counts the NUMBER TOTAL times the function was invoked (or had an attempted invocation), regardless of the result (success, error, or even excluding Thrttled requests that never reach the function) — it cannot distinguish between code errors, Throttling and performance problems; these distinctions require the dedicated metrics Errors, Throttles and Duration, respectively.

Incorrect. This mapping is incorrect: 'Competitions' measures to CONTAGEM of competing invocations (not code errors), 'IteratorAge' applies only to event sources based on STREAM and measures processing delay (not throttling in general), and 'Errors' measures faults at the code level (not performance/duration) — none of these mappings correspond correctly to the fault modes described.

Incorrect. Although a combined alarm could notify that 'something is wrong', the scenario explicitly requires DISTINGUIR between the three fault modes (each requiring a remedy) DIFERENTE: Code correction vs. increased competition vs. performance optimization); combining them in a single alarm with OR loses that distinction and would require further investigation to determine which of the three actually occurred — frustrating the stated objective.

dva-avc-212.text: A rule of Amazon EventBridge route events to a function Lambda The team realizes that, occasionally, the EventBridge FALHA when delivering an event to that target (e.g., the function of the Lambda returns a throttling error and the retry policy of the EventBridge — standard or custom — eventually exhausts your attempts, or the resource-based policy of the function does not grant invocation permission to EventBridge during a short window of a deployment). DeadLetterConfig configured no TARGET of a rule EventBridge specifically captures the events for which the EventBridge has exhausted its policy of retry (MaximumRetryAttempts/MaximumEventAgeInSeconds) without successfully delivering them to target — either failures caused by target errors (throttling) or failures in permission/delivery of itself EventBridge. The legacy configuration of 'DLQ' IN THE FUNCTION Lambda applies to PROPRIATE failures PROCESSAMENTO INVOLVING ASSISTANCE OF THE Function (after the EventBridge have already successfully delivered/invoked); it does NOT capture cases where the EventBridge IN SI fails to deliver the event to the target (e.g. for permission problems that prevent invocation, or exhaustion of retry on the side of the EventBridge) — for this it is necessary the DeadLetterConfig of itself TARGET of the EventBridge.

Lambda Destinations 'OnFailure' captures failures QUE OCORREM DEPOIS of the function to be INVOCADA with success, but the INVOCATION IN SI fail (e.g. the function code launches an exception); it does not capture faults of ENTREGA at the level of EventBridge which occur ANTES of/without a successful invocation (e.g., permission errors that prevent the EventBridge to invoke the function) — the DeadLetterConfig target of the rule of EventBridge cover this broader case.

Increasing the number of attempts may reduce (but not eliminate) the chance of exhaustion of withdrawals for TRANSITIONAL failures, but for failures PERSISTENTES (e.g.: a bad permission configuration that is not solved by itself) even the maximum number of attempts will eventually be exhausted, and the event would still be DESCARTADO SILENCIOSAMENTE without one DLQ set up — retreats alone do not provide PRESERVATION of events with failure for inspection/reprocessing.
